title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 76
paragraphs: When the barbarians had been laid low by the Greeks at Plataea, a woman approached — the concubine of Pharandates son of Teaspis, a Persian — coming over of her own free will from the enemy. When she perceived that the Persians had been destroyed and that the Greeks were victorious, she descended from her carriage and came up to the Lacedaemonians while they were still engaged in the slaughter. She had adorned herself with many gold ornaments, and her attendants likewise, and she had put on the finest of her robes. Seeing that Pausanias was directing everything there — being already familiar with his name and lineage, which she had heard often — she recognized Pausanias, took hold of his knees, and said: “O king of Sparta, deliver your suppliant from the slavery of the captive. For you have already done me a service by destroying these men, who have respect for neither demigods nor gods. I am by race of Cos, the daughter of Hegetorides son of Antagoras; and the Persian took me by force in Cos and kept me a prisoner.” He answered: “Woman, be of good courage — both because you are a suppliant, and also, if in addition it chances that you are speaking the truth and are the daughter of Hegetorides of Cos, who is bound to me as guest-friend more than any other man dwelling in those parts.” Having said this, he for the time put her in charge of the Ephors present; and afterwards he sent her to Aegina, where she herself wished to go.
